Free / First course

No-limit Texas hold’em / For beginners

Poker Foundations.

Learn to follow a hand and explain your next decision. Begin with the cards, then connect the action, the board and the reasons behind a bet.

Format
Six core lessons + starter practice
Pace
One small task per visit
Access
Free, no account needed

Your route through the course

  1. Cards, actions and the pot

    Name your legal actions, count an additional call and build the best five cards.

  2. Your starting hand in context

    Describe position and earlier action before judging two private cards.

  3. Your first decisions after the flop

    Name a made hand and a draw separately, then read the action.

  4. The turn, river and showdown

    Rebuild the best five after each new card and distinguish a call price from a reason to call.

  5. Your first range

    Separate known cards, possible opposing hands and assumptions about their frequency.

  6. Betting with a purpose

    Say which worse hands might call or better hands might fold, and compare betting with checking.

Each lesson has a short first pass, a question to explain and a practice situation with a repair link. The card builder, guided hand and betting rehearsal are there when you need them.

A-K with two shoves: the first decision is not the second.

In the recorded 12-round Stand Off account, I begin with about ten big blinds and A-K on the button. This review uses my archived v9 editing script and source-verification notes, which draw on my recorded narration and a camera-clock image. The public Episode 2 upload exists, but I have not independently checked that its current scene timing, graphics or every spoken word still matches the archived v9 package.

Tournament setting, as reported in the source packet: $200 entry, 30,000 starting chips, and a planned ICM-based payout to players surviving the end of round 12. A camera-clock reference in that packet places the main hand around round 10, with 17 of 78 entries remaining, at 3,000/6,000 blinds and a 6,000 big blind ante. These are source-packet claims, not an independently confirmed current tournament structure or calendar date.

  1. Decision 1, before the action changed. An early-position player raised to 15,000, another player called, and I flat-called on the button with A-K rather than shoving. My stack was approximately 61,000 chips. After the 15,000 call, about 46,000 remained. The v9 fact ledger lists my suits as A-clubs and K-diamonds from a camera still, but I have not reverified that still against the current public upload.
  2. Decision 2, after two shoves. The big blind shoved, the original raiser reshoved, and the middle caller folded. Both all-in players covered me according to my narration. My next decision was whether to call roughly 46,000 more and risk elimination. This was a different decision from whether to flat the first 15,000. The already-invested chips did not automatically justify another call.
  3. Showdown and immediate reaction. I called. My earlier account says the big blind showed K-K and the original raiser Q-Q. I lost and reported busting in round 10 without cashing. The source does not establish the full board, opponents' suits, exact effective stacks, or any prize amount from this event.
  4. Later hotel review, not solver proof. I first said I could not fold, then reconsidered after reflecting on the big blind's ability to call only 9,000 more before shoving instead. I inferred that a strong player might flat some hands with which they would otherwise call. That was my retrospective hypothesis about a range, not an independently validated restriction or a numerical ICM verdict.

What can be checked arithmetically: approximately 61,000 less 15,000 is about 46,000 chips; 15,000 to call less the big blind's posted 6,000 is 9,000 more; 61,000 at a 6,000 big blind is roughly 10.2 BB before the first call. The 6,000 big blind ante is a separate contribution, not another six thousand already covering the raise. These calculations do not reveal the players' actual ranges or determine whether the 46,000 call was correct.

Inspect the bounded record: download the archived-source A-K ledger (.json) and the offline consistency checker (.py). Both concern the source record, not the current video export. The structured record deliberately marks full boards, opponent suits, ICM results, exact payouts, verified current-cut chapters and human video sign-off as unavailable.

To check the ledger locally, save both files into the same folder and run py -3 portland-meadows-standoff-ak-gate.py --check portland-meadows-standoff-ak-source-ledger.json. Run py -3 portland-meadows-standoff-ak-gate.py --self-test to test six deliberately altered examples. Use python3 instead of py -3 on macOS or Linux. The checker uses only Python's standard library and neither uploads the record nor runs an AI model.

This is a short source review and reusable method for distinguishing an initial plan from a later decision. The longer Stand Off companion supplies the full narrative and source limits, without claiming the current video graphics or timecodes have passed review. The original production packet remains private. The separate Episode 1 companion documents the earlier Deepstack event. For editing standards, see From Hand Notes to a Poker Vlog.

Hand review / AI and human judgment

What can an AI solver actually tell me about a tournament hand?

Solver-style advice depends on the model and its inputs. In a live tournament, exact ranges, opponent incentives, payout effects, and even some remembered actions may be uncertain. Winning or losing a pot cannot settle whether the decision was good.

  1. Record the hand: Keep positions, stacks, blinds, board, action, and the information available at the time separate from later discoveries.
  2. Expose the assumptions: Identify which opponent ranges, reads, or tournament conditions are inferred rather than documented.
  3. Limit the conclusion: Use a modeled line to examine a decision, then state what the available record cannot prove. Do not present a retrospective explanation as an exact solver result.

For the underlying records, read the Portland Meadows six-four offsuit hand and my hand-review framework. I discuss the broader tension in When to Trust the AI vs. When to Trust Human Instinct.

The same evidence-first method informs my practical AI work in technology, including checking software even after automated tests pass. These tournament accounts do not claim complete, independently verified GTO or ICM solutions.
